summary: Italy is part of the Schengen Area: EU citizens travel freely, and Swiss and EEA nationals enter with a valid identity card or passport; nationals of the countries and territories on the EU's visa-exempt list (Annex II of Regulation (EU) 2018/1806) can stay up to 90 days in any 180-day period (the ETIAS travel authorisation is not yet in operation), and nationals of the countries on its visa-required list (Annex I) need a Schengen short-stay visa (standard fee €90 under the Visa Code). overstay.text: Unless the act is a more serious crime, a foreigner who enters or remains in Italy in breach of the Consolidated Immigration Act or of art. 1 of Law 68/2007 is punished with a fine of 5,000 to 10,000 euros. The same sanction as for not declaring presence applies to a foreigner who declared their presence and stayed beyond three months, or beyond the shorter period set in the entry visa. The re-entry ban after expulsion lasts not less than three and not more than five years, set by taking into account all the circumstances of the case.

driving.text: Italy is a party to the 1949 Geneva and the 1968 Vienna Conventions on Road Traffic (UN Treaty Collection). Italy's Highway Code (Legislative Decree 285/1992, art. 135) says holders of a driving licence issued by a country outside the EU or the EEA may drive in Italy the vehicles their licence covers, provided they have not been resident in Italy for more than a year and carry, together with the licence, an international driving permit or an official translation of the licence into Italian. Art. 186 treats a blood-alcohol level above 0.5 grams per litre as drunk driving. Art. 186-bis forbids driving after drinking alcohol, and fines a blood-alcohol level above zero, for drivers under 21 and in the first three years after obtaining a category B licence, drivers who carry passengers or goods as an occupation, and drivers of vehicles over 3.5 t, vehicles towing a trailer with a combined mass over 3.5 t, buses and other vehicles with more than eight passenger seats, and articulated vehicles. Canada's travel advice says you may drive for up to one year with a valid Canadian driver’s licence, accompanied by an international driving permit or a certified Italian translation of the licence. The UK government says a UK photocard driving licence can be used to drive in Italy.

The boundaries are usually marked ZTL in black on a yellow background; if you pass the sign, your registration number is likely to be caught on camera and you will be fined if you do not have a pass.

The UK FCDO says many major cities charge a small tourist tax, usually paid at your hotel and unlikely to be included in your booking. The rate varies by city and can depend on the hotel's star rating; hotels often ask for cash, so get a receipt.

The UK FCDO says that if you buy a public transport ticket from a kiosk or machine, you must validate it before you start your journey: officials patrol and issue on-the-spot fines for unvalidated tickets. Some buses and trams accept contactless payment on board.

faq.question: Do US citizens need a visa for Italy?
faq.answer: No. The United States is on the EU's visa-exempt list (Annex II of Regulation (EU) 2018/1806), whose nationals can stay up to 90 days in any 180-day period without a visa. Italy is among the countries that will require visa-exempt travellers to have an ETIAS travel authorisation, which is not yet in operation; the official ETIAS website gives the application fee as EUR 20.

faq.question: How much does an Italy Schengen visa cost?
faq.answer: The Schengen short-stay visa costs €90 for adults and €45 for children aged six to under 12. Under EU visa facilitation agreements, nationals of Armenia, Azerbaijan and Belarus pay €35 and nationals of Cabo Verde 75% of the standard fee. Italy's Foreign Ministry says a short stay means up to 90 days in any 180-day period, calculated as a single period for all European countries using the EES.

faq.question: Is ETIAS required to enter Italy?
faq.answer: ETIAS is currently not in operation and no applications are being collected; the EU will announce the start date several months before launch. The official ETIAS website gives the application fee as EUR 20.

faq.question: Does Italy have a digital nomad visa?
faq.answer: Italy's Consulate General in London lists a digital nomad visa for the self-employed only and a separate remote worker visa for subordinate workers. For the digital nomad visa it asks for proof of a recognised highly qualified profession; annual income of at least triple the minimum level (€8,500) set for exemption from participation in public health costs; suitable lodging; health insurance covering all hospital and medical costs for the entire stay; and at least six months' work experience in the field; and it says applications may take up to 120 days to process.

faq.question: How long can I stay in Italy without a visa?
faq.answer: Nationals of the countries on the EU's visa-exempt list can stay up to 90 days in any 180-day period, and Italy's Foreign Ministry says this is calculated as a single period for all European countries using the EES. EU law says no entry visa may be imposed on EU citizens; Swiss nationals enter on a valid identity card or passport under the EU–Swiss agreement, and the EEA Agreement incorporates the EU free movement directive.

levies.text: Provincial capitals, unions of municipalities and municipalities on regional lists of tourist resorts or art cities may introduce, by council resolution, a tax on people staying in accommodation in their territory. It is graduated by price, up to 5 euro per night of stay. Provincial capitals with tourist presences twenty times their residents may apply it up to the maximum set by art. 14(16)(e) of Decree-Law 78/2010. The accommodation manager is responsible for paying it, with a right of recourse against the guests.

levies.exemptions: Residents of the municipality; workers; commuting students; and family members of people who have paid the municipal property tax in the same municipality, who are treated as residents.
levies.text: Municipalities on minor islands may, instead of the tourist tax, introduce a landing contribution of up to EUR 2.50 for passengers who disembark on the island using scheduled or commercial carriers. The shipping and air companies collect it together with the ticket price. Municipalities may raise it to up to EUR 5 for certain periods. Residents, workers, commuting students and family members of people who paid the municipal property tax there do not pay it.

source.name: Normattiva — Legislative Decree 23/2011, art. 4 c.3-bis (contributo di sbarco)
source.instrument: D.Lgs. 14 marzo 2011, n. 23, art. 4, comma 3-bis

levies.feeText: Set by the municipality, up to EUR 2.50 per passenger disembarking on the minor island, as an alternative to the tourist tax; municipalities may raise it to up to EUR 5 for certain periods.
